articles.title: Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
articles.summary: Adobe’s sneaks can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.
articles.body: Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process. The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference. You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in. [Image: This Personality tab lets you manually adjust any of the traits that were generated for the character by talking to it. This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides far less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention. There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle. [Image: This still doesn’t really do Project Sight Span justice, but a video demonstration should take place at the Adobe Max sneaks keynote. Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward. Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects. [Image: Dragging your cursor around that square on the left changes the AI-generated audio as you’re listening to it. Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools. [Image: [Image: These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that might eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology. A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects. “Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told The Verge. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

articles.title: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments.
articles.body:
AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe.

Efforts to benchmark agents tasked with complex work show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0 shows Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and an effort by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy.

Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases.

Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.

“The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.”

On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity and Mercer.

Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple data sets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns.

To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents, and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Cursor.

However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming mid-tier frontier models at lower costs.

“We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said.

Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said.

Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data.

“My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

articles.title: Instagram's AI may catch teens lying about their age
articles.summary: Meta's AI age-estimation technology now scans Instagram accounts worldwide, placing millions of teens into stricter safety settings automatically.
articles.body: My own niece has told me for years that she and her friends could get around age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram when they were younger. They knew how easy it was to make themselves appear older online. And I suspect plenty of parents have heard similar stories. So when I heard that Meta was expanding its AI technology to identify teens who lie about their age, my first thought was, it's about time. On November 9, Meta announced a worldwide expansion of its AI age-estimation technology. The system looks for accounts that may belong to teenagers, even when someone has entered an adult birthday. Meta says the expansion will place millions more young users into Instagram's built-in Teen Account protections. The move comes as lawsuits and growing public pressure push Meta to take greater responsibility for protecting young users. After years of concerns about children getting around social media age restrictions, this could be one of the company's most significant attempts yet to address the problem. But how does Instagram's AI figure out someone's age? And can parents trust it to get things right? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 How Instagram AI age checks work For years, entering a birthday was one of the easiest ways to tell Instagram how old you were. The problem was that the app had to rely heavily on what someone told it. Now Meta is using artificial intelligence to look for clues that suggest an account belongs to someone under 18. Instead of relying solely on the birthday listed on a profile, the company's age-estimation technology analyzes account activity and other signals to estimate whether someone may be a teenager. Meta has previously explained that its age-detection technology can look for clues such as birthday celebrations, references to school grades and information shared in posts or comments. The company has also described separate technology that analyzes photos and videos to help identify accounts belonging to children under 13. According to the company, that technology examines general visual clues without using facial recognition or identifying specific people. The important thing to understand is that these systems estimate age. They don't establish someone's exact birthday. If Instagram's AI determines that an account likely belongs to someone between 13 and 17, the company can automatically apply Teen Account protections. That means a teenager who entered an adult birthday could suddenly find their account operating under stricter safety settings. What happens when Instagram identifies a teen? Instagram's Teen Accounts have been around since 2024. However, those protections depend on the platform correctly identifying younger users. The new worldwide expansion is designed to close that gap. When Meta identifies an account that likely belongs to a teenager, it can apply safeguards that include: Teens under 16 generally need parental permission to make built-in safety settings less restrictive. Instagram has also introduced 13+ content settings inspired by PG-13 movie ratings. Those filters are designed to reduce the amount of mature material younger users encounter. We previously covered how Instagram's PG-13 restrictions give parents more control over what teens see. Of course, no content filter catches everything. And these protections can only help if Instagram correctly identifies the accounts that need them. ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW Instagram's AI age checks are going worldwide Meta began testing AI technology to identify teens using adult birthdays in the United States in April 2025. The company later expanded the system to additional countries, including Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. In May 2026, Meta announced further expansion into the European Union and Brazil. Now the technology is going global. According to Meta, millions more teens will receive additional safety protections, even if they originally claimed to be adults. The company is also expanding age-detection technology on Facebook, with a similar rollout planned for Threads later in 2026. Meanwhile, Meta says it has started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia. With the right permissions, Apple's system can share someone's age range with participating apps. That gives Meta another way to check whether someone meets an app's age requirements. The big question is whether all this technology will finally make it harder for kids to get around the rules. Why Meta is finally getting serious about teen safety The timing of this announcement is worth paying attention to. For years, parents and child safety advocates have raised concerns about social media platforms and their effects on young users. Meanwhile, Meta has faced lawsuits alleging that its platforms contribute to harmful experiences for children and teenagers. Meta reportedly reached settlements worth up to approximately $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August 2026. The agreements address lawsuits brought by attorneys general over alleged harm to teens. Under those agreements, Meta committed to strengthening how it identifies teenagers and children younger than 13. The settlement also includes stronger controls for teens in participating U.S. jurisdictions, including a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram that requires parental permission to disable. Additional provisions address nighttime access and parental oversight. Those commitments are separate from the new worldwide AI expansion, although they reflect the broader pressure Meta faces. And there's an important point here. Meta has known for years that younger users sometimes enter false birthdays. The challenge has been figuring out how to identify them reliably. The company has introduced safety features over time. But public criticism and legal action have increased the pressure to show that those features actually work. Meta's latest announcement suggests the company is putting more resources behind age detection. The results will determine whether this becomes a meaningful turning point. We reached out to Meta for comment on its expanded AI age checks, but did not hear back before our deadline. Could Instagram's AI get someone's age wrong? That's another concern worth examining. AI can make mistakes, particularly when it tries to draw conclusions from someone's online activity. An adult might regularly post photos of younger relatives. Someone could also share old school pictures or birthday celebrations from years ago. That doesn't mean one post will automatically convince Instagram that an adult is a teenager. Meta uses multiple signals when making age estimates. However, mistakes remain possible. Meta says people who are incorrectly placed into Teen Account settings can take steps to verify their age and restore the appropriate settings. Depending on the situation, Instagram may require proof of age through identification or an age-estimation service. And there's another side to the problem. The technology could miss teenagers who successfully make their accounts appear to belong to adults. That's why parents should still review their children's account settings rather than assuming Instagram has correctly identified their age. Meta's November 9 announcement did not provide a new accuracy figure for the worldwide expansion. I'd like to see more information about how often the system gets these decisions right and how quickly people can correct mistakes. CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS What parents can expect from Meta Starting in November 2026, Meta says parents in the United States will begin seeing an informational video in their Instagram feeds. The video will explain how Meta identifies teenagers and places them into age-appropriate protections. It will also link to guidance from internet safety advocate Larry Magid, president and CEO of ConnectSafely. The guidance explains Meta's approach to identifying younger users and how parents can help ensure their children's ages are accurate. Parents worldwide can also access age-assurance resources through Meta's Family Center. For families, this creates an opportunity to have a conversation about why social media platforms ask for someone's age in the first place. Tips to help keep your teen safer on Instagram Even with stronger AI protections, I wouldn't leave everything up to Instagram. There are several practical steps parents can take right now. 1. Check your teen's birthday on Instagram Ask your teen to open Instagram and go to their profile. Tap the menu, open Accounts Center, then look for Personal details and Birthday. Make sure the birthday is accurate. Instagram may require verification if someone attempts to change an account's age from under 18 to an adult age. 2. Review their account privacy settings Open Instagram's settings and look for the account privacy controls. Check whether the account is private and review who can follow your teen. Also review who can send messages. You may find that some protections are already enabled through Teen Accounts. 3. Turn on parental supervision Instagram's Family Center gives parents additional tools for managing a teen's experience. Parental supervision requires both the parent and teen to agree to the connection. Once connected, parents can review available safety controls and manage certain account restrictions. 4. Review screen time controls Instagram offers daily usage reminders and additional restrictions for teens. Parents can also use supervision settings to manage screen time. On an iPhone, open Settings, then Screen Time to review available app limits. For Android devices, Google Family Link offers parental controls and device management options. 5. Check the content settings Instagram's 13+ content setting is designed to limit material that may be inappropriate for teenagers. Parents can review these protections and choose stricter settings where available. Remember that filters may still miss content, so it's worth asking your teen what regularly appears in their feed. 6. Talk about why age restrictions exist This may be the most useful step. Ask your teen whether they have ever felt tempted to enter an older birthday to unlock features or avoid restrictions. Explain that providing the correct age helps Instagram apply protections intended for younger users. And make sure they know they can talk to you if they encounter something uncomfortable online. Kurt's key takeaways It's about time. My own niece told me years ago how easily she and her friends could get around the age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram. And I remember wondering why these platforms weren't doing more about it. Now, with lawsuits mounting and public pressure growing, Meta is finally taking a bigger step to address the problem. I'm glad to see it, but I want to know how well this AI actually works. Will it catch teens who lie about their age? And what happens when it gets someone's age wrong? Parents have been asking for better protections for years. It's time for Meta to show that these changes are making kids safer online. Do you think Meta would be taking these steps without years of public pressure and lawsuits, or has the company finally realized it needs to do more to protect children online? articles.title: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
articles.summary: Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells.
articles.body: Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments. AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was released last year. While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell. The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed. AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases — huge data repositories that map and catalog individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model. Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab. For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told The Verge. Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told The Verge that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital. Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “virtual cells,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems. Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide Atlas covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September. Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research. The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been experimenting with drug design and given Claude a wet lab, while OpenAI has been mowing down an impressive amount of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields.

articles.title: 'I think we're on the brink of a revolution': Google researcher hails AI agents after they found what looks like an ancient Maya site in Mexico
articles.summary: AI tech is quickly transforming many different fields of research, including archaeology, as this discovery shows.
articles.body:

AI agents have found what looks like an undiscovered Maya site

The discovery came from a scan of LiDAR data collected by Mexico

Experts are now investigating the site that the AI has flagged up

While some of AI's 'talents' — like putting together decent-looking restaurant menus — could legitimately be called into question, there's no doubt that these bots and agents excel at spotting patterns in vast troves of data, and the latest evidence comes from the potential discovery of a hidden Maya archaeological site in Mexico.

Google researcher Pietro Miotti described having a "random thought on vacation" about how AI agents might be used to sift through LiDAR datasets — topographical maps of Earth's terrain, captured from space satellites.

LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) lasers can cut through cloud cover and forest canopies, enabling researchers to find shapes in the landscape that aren't visible to the naked eye (or in landscapes that aren't even accessible to archaeologists).

Miotti tasked 48 agents from different AI apps with scouring through a NASA database of LiDAR information collected across Peru, and the AI came back with multiple hits on structures that could be buildings. A second scan by the agents identified one particular site that hasn't yet been mentioned in scientific literature.

My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site in Mexico, using LiDAR data from a NASA dataset.72 hours from a random thought on vacation to a reply from Mexico's national archaeology institute.What a time to be alive… — @PietroMiotti (November 10, 2026) Voir le tweet original

My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site in Mexico, using LiDAR data from a NASA dataset.72 hours from a random thought on vacation to a reply from Mexico's national archaeology institute.What a time to be alive…

The AI assistance didn't stop there: Miotti's bot helpers told him who he should get in touch with about the discovery (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History or INAH), and then composed an email (in Spanish) to the relevant agency, including details of the find and where on the map it's located.

Representatives from INAH got in touch, and the experts there are investigating further: a real result, in 72 hours. The site's status as an ancient Maya site hasn't been confirmed yet, but it looks like a promising lead, and one that was made possible by AI.

"I think we're on the brink of a revolution across every science, not just coding, physics and math," says Miotti. "And at this point we should LiDAR the entire planet and let agents help us find the rest."

Miotti still wasn't finished there, and got Gemini to generate an image of how the site may have looked in 700 CE — when the Maya people were actually living there. In the modern era, some serious exploring can be done from a computer through a team of AI bots, as well as out in the field.

articles.title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
articles.summary: Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends.﻿
articles.body: Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more. “Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.” [Video: Google Labs Tabletop AI] Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.

articles.title: OpenAI's quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Sales of $10B represents an almost 50% jump from revenue of $6.7 billion the company recorded in the second quarter.
articles.body:
OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources.

If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.

OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said.

OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses.

But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion . OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users , but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans.

Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude-maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth.

OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks.

OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon , said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October.

(Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.)

None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open-source AI labs, especially those from China.

articles.title: Is Jensen Huang’s bad behavior more commonplace than it seems? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: “There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,” an investment intel consultant said.
articles.body:
The AI industry is still reeling from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s honeypot scandal, but some in the industry see it as an issue that’s much larger than one man.

The Chinese government has been active in economic espionage for decades, and with semiconductors at the center of the AI boom, there’s intense pressure to infiltrate any company involved. At the same time, many of the executives getting rich off that boom have made themselves easy targets.

As CEO of investment intel firm Heron Intelligence, Nate Singer has a unique view into the problem. His firm works on corporate due diligence: Essentially, making sure companies know the relevant dirt before making a major acquisition or executive hire. And while the Nvidia case is particularly severe, Singer says there are lots of similar cases in the semiconductor industry that have stayed under the radar.

“We’ve got former employees talking about behavior at senior executive levels,” Singer told TechCrunch, saying executives are “really crossing lines that should not be crossed.”

In a widely circulated LinkedIn post , Singer detailed one case in which a CEO’s wife made an unexpected board room appearance, “screaming about her husband and another company exec flying around in the corporate jet with a couple young ladies (who also turned out to be state-sponsored actors).”

It’s an alarming story, but an unfortunately common one. Singer says he’s seen at least three reports of similar cases, and suspects many more have gone unreported.

“There’s a lot more than this one woman,” Singer said. “They are embedded in these companies.”

Semiconductor companies are already big targets for international trade secret theft. There have been dozens of prosecutions for similar cases in recent years, including a case involving the fabrication powerhouse TSMC in 2006.

In 2017, four executives at an unnamed “Bay Area semiconductor equipment manufacturer” were charged with stealing trade secrets for use at a competing company in China. According to the indictment, the technology in question “related to the high-volume manufacturing of semiconductor wafers to be used in lighting and electronic devices, such as flat screen televisions and smart phones.“

Any sexual elements in such cases rarely become public, in part because of the severe consequences for executives and their companies. But according to Singer, the ongoing threat has become a kind of open secret in the industry.

“There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,” he told TechCrunch.

articles.title: Dani García, experto en IA, revela lo que tienes que hacer antes de usarla: "Cásate con ella"
articles.standfirst: El profesional en el sector lo desvela paso a paso
articles.summary: El profesional en el sector lo desvela paso a paso
articles.body: La tecnología continúa evolucionando a pasos alucinantes, sobre todo, la inteligencia artificial (IA). Una herramienta que, prácticamente forma parte del día a día de gran variedad de ámbitos. Sin embargo, su uso, en ocasiones, es indebido. En este contexto, Dani García, experto en IA y creador de contenido al respecto, reveló en uno de sus últimos vídeos lo que hay que hacer con ella antes de usarla, llegando a la conclusión que hay que “casarse” con ella. García comentó que “no” hay que escribirle a ninguna IA: “Sobre todo si la respuesta que te da no te sirve, porque el fallo está mucho antes de empezar a escribirle”, apostilló para justificar esta expresión. Lo primero que hay que hacer es elegir una IA: “Casarse con ella, así de claro. Ya sea Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, al final da igual cual acabes escogiendo. No cambies de IA cada vez que veas en TikTok un vídeo diciéndote que otra IA es mejor. Al final no le vas a sacar partido a ninguna, pero da igual cuál elijas si al final le hablas como si estuvieras buscando en Google”. “La IA no es tonta. Le falta contexto. Dile qué necesitas, para qué lo necesitas y cómo lo quieres. Y si no te convence, corrígela ahí mismo, sin irte a otro chat”, continuó manifestando Dani García. Por último, desveló lo que “casi nadie” hace y “marca” la diferencia: “Pídele que te pregunte. Le escribes lo que necesitas y al final le dices, hazme todas las preguntas que necesitas para hacerlo perfecto, porque ella sabe mejor que tú lo que le falta. Tú le contestas y el resultado que te da ahora no tiene nada que ver con el resultado que te daba antes”.

articles.title: Congress to call Jensen Huang in to answer for alleged Chinese spy affair | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has until the end of the day Wednesday to answer a call from House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on his affair with alleged Chinese spy.
articles.body:
Congress is gearing up to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to answer their questions about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy , Bloomberg reports , citing two House Republicans.

The report comes a week after House Republicans Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent a letter to Huang asking him to appear before their committees for a joint, closed-door briefing in regards to his relations with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy.

House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that Huang has until the end of the day to respond to the request. If he doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed, said Moolenaar.

Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Wednesday said his committee is preparing a subpoena for Huang to send if he doesn’t respond.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth | TechCrunch
articles.summary: CoreWeave is increasingly asking customers to pay upfront, borrowing against specific contracts, and even looking to short-term deals that could lead to higher prices, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings.
articles.body:
CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices.

The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue.

CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense.

“We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call.

Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion.

CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware.

Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts.

Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge.

CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices.

The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator.

“We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said.

CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money.

While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a tradeoff. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all.

Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return.

In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand.

TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

articles.title: Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure
articles.summary: Santosh Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, will be stepping down from his role.
articles.body:
A key figure in Meta’s growth into a social media and tech industry powerhouse is leaving the company.

Santosh Janardhan, the company’s longtime head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, will be stepping down, Meta told TechCrunch. He will be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined the company as vice president of infrastructure earlier this year, the company added. Previous to coming aboard at Meta, Brown spent 19 years at Amazon, where he focused on compute, cloud, and AI, his LinkedIn shows .

It sounds like Janardhan will remain at Meta for a little bit, although he is expected to leave next year. “Santosh will stay on for transition and he is moving into an advisory role on Meta Compute,” said a Meta representative.

Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, helped the firm grow into the massive internet presence that it is today. Bloomberg originally reported Janardhan’s departure, citing an internal memo that had recently been circulated. It’s unclear why Janardhan is stepping down from the role. The memo did not specify the reasons for his departure and Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarity on the issue. However, Janardhan’s memo apparently cited the need to “pass the baton.”

In recent years, the company’s investment in infrastructure has exploded , as it seeks to keep up with its competitors in the AI race. Earlier this year, Janardhan was tasked with leading Meta Compute , the company initiative to scale its data center investments and strategy.

articles.title: Why the data center you dread might never even be built
articles.summary: he data center boom looks huge on paper, but how much will actually get built? On this episode of Equity, an energy expert breaks down the projects likely to happen and the ones that never will.
articles.body:
The data center boom is running into serious real-world obstacles, from widespread local opposition and permitting delays to a scramble for electricity . Before those challenges even come into play, though, there’s a more basic problem: A lot of the projects being announced may never get built in the first place. With billions of dollars in AI infrastructure investment at stake, separating realistic projects from speculative ones is becoming increasingly important.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Rebecca Bellan and Tim De Chant are joined by Brent Nelson , senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , to separate the data center projects that are likely to get built from the ones that may never get off the ground.

articles.title: United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
articles.summary: United will restrict unauthorized AI agents from booking flights on its airline, citing privacy and regulatory issues.
articles.body: United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns. The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives. While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal. Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

articles.title: Hugging Face cofounder: Open-weight AI models were 'our savior'
articles.summary: Hugging Face cofounder Thomas Wolf says open-weight models saved the company from the summer's OpenAI hack.
articles.body:
When OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) research models went rogue and hacked open-source AI site Hugging Face over the summer, cofounder and chief science officer Thomas Wolf says the company couldn't rely on closed models, such as those from OpenAI or Anthropic, to defend itself.

Instead, he told Deirdre Bosa, the company had to turn to an open-weight AI model developed by Chinese company Z.ai to determine what was happening during the attack and cut it off.

The episode turned on its head the thinking that open models were somehow dangerous.

"Traditionally, let's say last year, people had this view that open-weight models might be dangerous, and actually they turned out in our case to be our savior," Wolf said.

Open-weight models are models that developers make available free for users to download, customize, and run on their own systems.

The companies that develop them, including China's Alibaba ( BABA ), DeepSeek, Z.AI, and others, make money by charging customers who lack the necessary hardware to run the models to access them on their own computers.

Open-weight models, especially those from China, have quickly gained in popularity among developers and enterprises.

The software is generally less expensive to run than leading closed models, and can be tuned to a customer's needs.

When OpenAI's models attacked Hugging Face, Wolf says the company couldn't use closed-weight models because their built-in guardrails wouldn't allow the firm to analyze the relevant hacking data.

But the open-weight model from Z.ai, like most open-weight models, allowed Hugging Face to adjust its guardrails, helping stop the attack.

"I think what we saw in the whole summer was people realizing that …everyone can't rely on these two labs [OpenAI and Anthropic] to protect themselves," Wolf said.

"So we need a lot more tools to protect ourselves, and open-weight models are gonna be one of the major…tools."

articles.title: Nvidia stock drops as board reportedly weighs Jensen Huang’s future
articles.summary: Nvidia shares dropped sharply in after-hours trading on Wednesday after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a company executive and that the board is meeting to discuss his future.
articles.body: Nvidia shares dropped sharply in after-hours trading on Wednesday after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a company executive and that the board is meeting to discuss his future. Nvidia shares (NVDA) tumbled more than 9% before trimming some losses and trading down 7.2% as of 7 p.m. ET as investors digested the developments. Shares of the world’s second-most-valuable company fell after The New York Times reported Huang had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, and the Wall Street Journal subsequently reported the Nvidia board is preparing to oust Huang, who co-founded the company three decades ago. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the new reports. Days earlier, Nvidia’s board said it would investigate whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” amid reports that he had a separate relationship with a woman US officials believe to be a Chinese spy. Huang on Sunday apologized for an extramarital affair, although he did not name the other party. Huang is without a clear No. 2 if the board decides to remove him, with the founder having previously said he does not believe in succession planning. “Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” he told Bloomberg in 2023. “So for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.” Investors are weighing the outlook for the chipmaker that’s been at the center of the AI boom if Huang is ousted from his role. The CEO has been one of AI’s most steadfast cheerleaders and funders, and investors have flocked to Nvidia shares because of his vision for the tech boom. Nvidia shares dropped 9.5% across Monday and Tuesday after Huang’s weekend admission of extramarital affair and news of the Nvidia board’s investigation. Shares rebounded Wednesday during trading, rising 2.9%, before tumbling in after-hours trading and erasing those gains. Nvidia shares were down 27% from a peak in early October as of the market close on Wednesday, before the sharp after-hours decline. Nvidia pioneered graphics processing units, which are semiconductor chips that are critical for AI. The company’s chips are used to power AI models, from OpenAI’s ChatGPT to Anthropic’s Claude. Nvidia is also a major player in backing massive infrastructure deals for the AI buildout. The drop in Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.9% and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% as of 7 p.m ET. While Nvidia shares tumbled, shares of other major semiconductor chipmakers moved higher. Advanced Micro Devices shares (AMD) rose 4.5% as of 7 p.m. ET, while Broadcom shares (AVGO) rose 2.9%. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.summary: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
articles.body:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported.

The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.

November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed .

November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote . “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.
